title: Unmold a tart from a loose-bottom pan: stand it on a cake stand and lower the ring away level
instruction: Take the tart out of its pan.
context: Baking at home is one of the most common household activities, loose-bottom fluted tart pans are standard home bakeware, and every tart baked in one ends with this move. A tart cannot be turned out upside down like a cake, because its crust and topping would break, and lifted by its rim the pan comes up whole, because the ring's inward bottom lip holds the loose base. Instead the cook holds the pan only by the outer rim, stands the base, centered, on something narrower than the base (America's Test Kitchen uses a can; here a small cake stand, so the tart ends ready to serve), and lowers the ring away level with both hands, so it drops to the counter and leaves the tart on its base, untouched. A ring lowered unevenly cocks, and its fluted wall can lever into the baked crust edge and break it. A base set off center can tip the tart off the stand.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A 24 cm (9.5-inch) fluted tart pan with a removable bottom, tinned steel, stands on the table centered at x 22.5, y 0: a ring whose wall is 2.6 cm tall with 30 flutes 2 mm deep, an inward bottom lip 1.25 cm wide (inner radius 10.6 cm, 4 mm thick) and a top rim; real pans have a 3 mm rolled rim, and here it is widened to a flat lip 1.2 cm wide (out to 26.7 cm across, 4 mm thick) so a gripper can pinch it; the ring weighs 150 g. The pan's loose base, a 23.4 cm steel disk 3 mm thick weighing 100 g, rests on the ring's bottom lip, and on it sits a baked tart 23.3 cm across and 2 cm tall with a fluted golden crust edge and a yellow filling, 450 g. A small plain white ceramic pedestal cake stand, 7 cm tall with an 11 cm top (narrower than the base and the ring's 21.2 cm bottom opening) on a 5 cm stem and a 9 cm foot, stands fixed on the table at x 41.5, y 0. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Doing nothing scores 0. Three events, watched over the whole run, score 0 for good, each counted once it holds for 2 control steps in a row, so a one-step physics pop does not count. First, a gripper touching the tart: its palm or a finger in contact with the tart's top, side or crust edge. Contact is judged by the gripper's own shape (boxes fitted to the YAM's collision meshes, with the fingers at their present opening) coming within 2 mm of the tart, which allows for the solver's resting gap and the box fit. A hand hovering over the tart more than 2 mm away does not count. The tart is never to be touched, because a finger can leave a mark in the filling or a dent in the crust. Second, the tart tilted past 20 degrees, which only happens when it slides on its base or falls against the stand's edge. Third, the tart shifted more than 5 mm across its base or lifted off it: it sits there by friction, so only a hand or the ring shoving its crust edge moves it that far. The sim's tart is rigid, so contact and shifting are proxies for a finger mark or a dented edge; a real trial checks the video for any finger on the tart and photographs the fluted edge before and after. At the end the score is 0 unless the base, with the tart on it, rests still on the cake stand: its center within 3 cm of the stand's axis, which keeps the load well inside the stand's 5.5 cm top radius; within 5 degrees of level, a 1 cm drop at the base's edge; its bottom within 5 mm of the stand's top, so it rests on the stand rather than being held above it. A real trial measures the offset with a ruler and the level with a phone inclinometer. Then 0.25 if the ring is still on (the base on its bottom lip) or a gripper is still touching the ring or the base, by the same contact check. The base is on the stand, but the job is not finished: a hand still holding the pan can lift the ring back or drag the base off center as it moves away, and whether the ring and base stay put on their own is only known once they are let go. The quarter is for getting the base centered on the stand. 0 if the ring is let go but not flat on the table around the stand (its bottom within 5 mm of the table, within 5 degrees of level, the stand inside its 21.2 cm bottom opening): a ring caught on the stand or the tart was dropped partway, still against the crust. 0.5 if the ring ever tilted past 6 degrees while sliding down past the crust, the 1.7 cm stretch where its bottom is 5 mm or more below where it holds the base and its top is still above the base's bottom (judged over each step's travel, tilted at both ends of the step). 6 degrees leans the top of the 2.6 cm wall 2.7 mm inward, deeper than the 2 mm flutes, so the wall can lever into the crust edge. The tilt is the proxy for that break; a real trial reads it from a phone inclinometer taped to the lip and checks the edge photos. The tart is out but its edge was put at risk, so half. Otherwise 1.0: unmolded level and let go, with no gripper touching the ring, base or tart. Letting go is required because the job ends with the tart standing free on its stand, ready to serve; where the arms end does not matter. Success is a full score held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: Put the base back in the ring and a fresh baked tart shell (or the README's 450 g weighted card disk) on it, set the pan back at its spot and check the cake stand is at its spot.
fidelity: Full-size 24 cm pan; the cake stand is fixed; the tart is 450 g (a real filled one is 600 to 900 g) so two pinch grips on the lip carry it reliably. The rolled rim is widened to a 1.2 cm flat lip for the grippers. The ring's colliders are 24 straight segments, the wall's flutes are drawn but its collider is round, and the tart is one rigid body: crust damage is scored from proxies (ring tilt, finger contact, the tart shifting); a real trial photographs the crust edge for breaks.
